opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it is just that the infrastructure and the recipes weren't there yet. Pre-training has had years of people grinding on it: we know the scaling laws, we know how to keep thousands of chips busy, we know what a good data mix looks like. RL on language models in this modern sense, where you're giving the model verifiable tasks and letting it learn from its own attempts, really only started working convincingly fairly recently. When something is new, you don't immediately throw a pre-training-sized budget at it. You run small experiments, you figure out what breaks, you build confidence that the curves keep going up before you scale.

There's also a real engineering asymmetry. Pre-training is a beautifully simple loop: stream tokens in, compute loss, update. RL is much messier. You have to generate rollouts, which is inference-heavy and has very different hardware characteristics. You need environments, graders, sandboxes for code execution, all of which have to be reliable at scale. If your reward signal is a bit off, the model will happily find the exploit rather than learn the skill you wanted. So a lot of the bottleneck early on wasn't compute, it was the quality and diversity of tasks and rewards. Throwing ten times more compute at a narrow set of environments doesn't buy you much.

And honestly, I think it's changing quickly. Once people saw that RL on top of a strong base model gives you these big jumps in reasoning and in agentic capability, the incentive to scale it up became obvious. My expectation is that the ratio shifts a lot, and that we'll look back on this period as the point where RL compute was still tiny relative to where it ends up. The base model gives you the priors, but RL is where you teach it to actually do long, hard, useful work, and there's a lot of headroom there.

r001.rationale: The response says labs ran small experiments and built confidence that results would scale, but it does not clearly identify confidence in reinforcement learning’s compute efficiency as the reason for delaying larger investments.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the engineering requirements of RL and pre-training and describes RL’s capability gains, but does not say RL is more amenable to iterative capability development.

r003.rationale: It predicts that the compute ratio will shift substantially and that RL compute will grow far beyond its current small share.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's less about any single bottleneck and more about where the marginal unit of compute was most reliably paying off.

For most of the last few years, pre-training was the sure thing. You had scaling laws that were almost embarrassingly predictable. You put in ten times the compute, you got a known improvement in loss, and that improvement showed up as broadly better capability across basically everything. When you're a lab deciding where to spend a very expensive cluster, that kind of predictability is incredibly attractive. RL just didn't have that story. It was finicky, it was reward-hacky, and it wasn't obvious that the gains would generalize beyond the narrow thing you trained on.

The second thing is that RL at scale has a bunch of prerequisites that only recently got solved. You need a base model that's good enough that it actually produces correct trajectories some reasonable fraction of the time, otherwise you're just sampling noise and there's no signal to reinforce. You need environments and verifiers, which is a real engineering investment. Things like code and math are nice because you can check the answer, but building those pipelines out and making them robust takes time. And you need the infrastructure to handle very long rollouts, lots of sampling, inference-heavy workloads that look quite different from a pre-training run. A lot of the systems work was built around dense forward-backward passes, not around generating hundreds of thousands of tokens and then scoring them.

And then there's just the fact that the field hadn't yet seen the proof point. Until someone demonstrated that RL on reasoning tasks produces these clean, scaling-law-like improvements, it was rational to be cautious. Once that evidence came in, I think you've seen the allocation shift fairly quickly. My expectation is that the ratio looks very different a year or two from now, and that in retrospect it'll seem obvious that RL should have had far more compute all along. But hindsight makes the ordering look cleaner than it felt at the time.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training had predictable compute returns, while RL lacked comparable evidence; it also says labs became more willing to allocate compute after RL showed scaling-like improvements.

r002.rationale: It contrasts pre-training’s broad gains with RL’s initially narrow and uncertain gains, but does not say RL is more amenable to iterative capability development.

r003.rationale: It predicts the compute allocation ratio will look very different within a year or two and says the shift has already begun.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that pre-training was a recipe that worked reliably. You could put more compute into it, predict roughly how much better the model would get, and get improvements across a huge range of tasks. That’s a very attractive investment compared with reinforcement learning, where you have to figure out what to reward, how to generate useful experience, and how to keep the model from exploiting your reward signal.

There’s also a bootstrapping problem. If the model almost never produces a successful solution, reinforcement learning has very little signal to work with. Pre-training gives you a model that can already do enough interesting things that you can start selecting and reinforcing the good trajectories.

So I wouldn’t interpret the historical compute split as evidence that reinforcement learning is inherently less useful. It might just reflect where we were in the sequence: first build a sufficiently capable starting point, then figure out how to get it to improve through experience. The question is whether you can make that second process as reliable and scalable as pre-training.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training was reliable and RL still needs to become reliable and scalable, but it does not explain that labs delayed large RL compute investments until they had confidence in algorithms’ compute efficiency.

r002.rationale: It describes using RL to improve a capable starting model through experience, but does not state that RL is more amenable to iterative capability development than pre-training.

r003.rationale: It raises whether RL can become reliable and scalable, but does not predict that RL’s relatively small share of compute spending will end soon.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that pre-training was a very reliable way to turn compute into better models. You had this enormous supply of text, a straightforward objective, and scaling laws that gave you some confidence about what you’d get from a bigger run. If you had more compute, the obvious thing to do was to train a larger model on more data.

With reinforcement learning, you have to build the thing that tells the model whether it did well. That’s relatively easy for something like a math problem where you can check the answer, but much harder for a task like doing research. And if your reward signal is imperfect, spending more compute can just make the model better at exploiting that imperfection.

There’s also a capability threshold. The model needs some chance of discovering a good solution before you can reinforce it. If it never succeeds, you don’t get much learning signal. So pre-training was doing two jobs: making the model useful directly, and giving it the capabilities that make reinforcement learning productive.

I’d expect that balance to shift as the base models get stronger and we get better at building environments where they can try things and receive useful feedback. The historical allocation doesn’t necessarily tell you what the optimal allocation will be going forward.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training was a reliable use of compute and describes challenges with RL rewards, but it does not explain that labs delayed large RL investments pending confidence in the algorithms’ compute efficiency.

r002.rationale: The response says RL can use feedback from attempts and becomes more productive as models strengthen, but it does not clearly distinguish RL as more amenable to iterative capability development than pre-training.

r003.rationale: The response expects the balance to shift but gives no timeframe or claim that RL’s relatively small compute share will not persist for long.
